title: Bulk RNA-seq Differential Expression Analysis with DESeq2 on the Airway Dataset
goal: Perform and validate a differential gene expression analysis on a public bulk RNA-seq dataset using RStudio, R, Bioconductor, and DESeq2. The workflow will include data inspection, quality control, statistical modelling, identification of differentially expressed genes, generation of publication-quality visualizations, and critical review of the analytical results with assistance from Claude.
context: I regularly perform bulk RNA-seq analyses as part of my work in computational biology. This workflow demonstrates a typical differential gene expression analysis using a public dataset, beginning with dataset inspection and quality assessment and ending with statistically validated results and publication-quality visualizations. Claude will be used to assist with code review, troubleshooting, and interpretation while I make the final analytical decisions.

session_goal_achievement.Why or why not: Yes, because Claude provided code that integrated well into my workflow, and I was able to complete the analysis on time with Claude's assistance.

Step 1.step_name: Inspect the dataset and define the biological comparison
Step 1.step_action: Load the airway dataset and required libraries, extract the count matrix and sample metadata, and inspect their basic structure. Review the public bulk RNA-seq count matrix and sample metadata. Confirm the sample groups, identify the biological comparison to be tested, and check whether the dataset is suitable for differential gene expression analysis. Ask Claude to review the proposed comparison and identify possible issues with the study design.

nodes.label: Load analysis packages and the airway dataset
nodes.detail: In RStudio (Minnesota_final.Rmd), the participant narrates his plan to analyze the public airway Bioconductor dataset with DESeq2, then loads DESeq2, ggplot2, ggrepel, pheatmap, RColorBrewer, org.Hs.eg.db, AnnotationDbi, apeglm and other libraries, followed by data(airway).

nodes.label: Extract the count matrix and sample metadata objects
nodes.detail: The participant extracts the raw count matrix via assay(se) and the sample metadata via colData(se), confirming in the Environment pane that counts is a 63,677 x 8 matrix and metadata is a DFrame with 8 samples.

nodes.label: Inspect metadata structure and confirm data integrity
nodes.detail: Using str(), head(), and table(metadata$dex), the participant identifies the treatment (dex), cell-line, and Run/sample columns, confirms 4 treated vs. 4 untreated samples, verifies colnames(counts) == rownames(metadata) are all TRUE, and checks per-sample library sizes with summary(colSums(counts)) before moving into the numbered workflow.

nodes.label: Write the biological background of the airway dataset
nodes.detail: Under a new '## Step 1' header, the participant writes prose describing the airway smooth muscle cell lines, their relevance to asthma, and the published GEO comparison of dexamethasone-treated versus untreated controls, framing the biological motivation for the analysis.

nodes.label: Define the experimental groups, comparison, and the DESeq2 design formula
nodes.detail: The participant states the two groups (treated 'trt' vs. untreated 'untrt', 4 samples each), identifies cell line as a confounding variable that must be controlled for, and writes out the intended design formula (~ cell + dex) that will be used to construct the DESeq2 object in the next step.

Step 2.step_name: Import and validate the RNA-seq data
Step 2.step_action: Import the bulk RNA-seq count matrix and sample metadata into RStudio. Verify that the sample identifiers match between the count matrix and metadata, check for missing values or duplicated sample names, and construct the DESeq2 dataset object. Ask Claude to review the validation process and suggest any additional quality checks before proceeding.

nodes.label: Re-import the saved count/metadata CSVs and re-validate the data
nodes.detail: The participant reads airway_counts.csv and airway_metadata.csv from disk via read.csv(row.names=1) to validate the data exactly as it will be loaded downstream, re-confirms colnames(counts)==rownames(metadata) are all TRUE, and checks any(is.na(counts)) is FALSE with no duplicated sample IDs.

nodes.label: Construct the DESeqDataSet object
nodes.detail: Using the validated counts, metadata, and the ~ cell + dex design formula from Step 1, the participant calls DESeqDataSetFromMatrix() to build the dds object, noting the resulting factor-conversion warning is expected and harmless, producing the validated dataset needed for downstream QC and DE analysis.

Step 3.step_action: Examine library sizes, count distributions, and sample relationships to identify potential low-quality samples or outliers. Apply an appropriate low-count gene filtering rule, transform the count data for visualization, and use PCA and sample-distance plots to assess whether samples cluster according to the expected biological groups. Ask Claude to review the quality-control strategy and help interpret any unusual sample patterns.

nodes.label: Filter low-count genes and confirm factor levels
nodes.detail: The participant filters to genes with rowSums(counts(dds)) >= 10, reducing 63,677 to 22,369 genes, then relevels dex so 'untrt' is the reference and converts cell to a factor, preparing dds for accurate downstream contrasts.

nodes.label: Apply variance-stabilizing transformation and assess sample distances
nodes.detail: The participant runs vst(dds, blind=FALSE) to produce vsd for visualization (explaining raw counts cannot be used directly since their variance depends on the mean), computes a sample-to-sample distance matrix, and renders a pheatmap that shows two clear clusters separating treated from untreated samples.

nodes.label: Ask Claude for PCA code that fits the existing script
nodes.detail: The participant opens the Claude desktop app (title 'Eine nachtliche Jam-Session', model 'Sonnet 5') in an agentic Cowork-style session, uploads the current Minnesota_final.Rmd, and asks for PCA code to check sample clustering by treatment and cell line that fits seamlessly into his existing flow.

nodes.label: Insert PCA plotting code directly into the R script
nodes.detail: Claude uses its file-editing tool to open the uploaded .Rmd, locates the empty PCA chunk right after the sample-distance heatmap, inserts a plotPCA()-based ggplot2 block colored by dex and shaped by cell line using the existing vsd object, and shares the updated file back with an explanation of the design choices.

nodes.label: Run the PCA code and interpret the clustering result
nodes.detail: The participant copies/keeps Claude's PCA code in the .Rmd, runs it in RStudio, and interprets the resulting plot showing treatment separating samples along PC1 (48% variance) and cell line varying along PC2 (23% variance), concluding treatment is the dominant source of variation.

user_response.label: adopt
user_response.reasoning: In c3, the participant asks for the PCA code, so it should be considered as the source node of this collaboration. Then the user directly adopts the code provided by Claude (c4) and satisfies with the result, so the target node is c4 and the label is adopt.

nodes.label: Ask Claude for a post-filtering library-size bar plot
nodes.detail: The participant asks the same Claude desktop chat for one code block making a bar plot of library sizes/total read counts post-filtering, to check for sequencing-depth outliers.

nodes.label: Insert the library-size bar-plot code after the filtering chunk
nodes.detail: Claude locates the pre-filtering chunk in the uploaded .Rmd, inserts a ggplot2 bar-plot block (colSums of the filtered dds, colored by dex) right after it, and shares the updated file with a rationale for using the post-filter dds.

nodes.label: Run the library-size plot and confirm no outlier samples
nodes.detail: The participant runs the returned code in RStudio and confirms no sample shows a drastically different total read count, concluding library sizes are comparable with no samples to flag or exclude.

user_response.label: adopt
user_response.reasoning: So in c6, the participant does ask the AI for the library-size bar plot, which make c6 the source node. And the user adopts the AI code (c7) directly, and he also confirms no outlier samples at around 33:35, the label is correct.

Step 4.step_name: Run differential gene expression analysis with DESeq2
Step 4.step_action: Fit the DESeq2 model using the validated count matrix and experimental design. Estimate size factors and dispersion parameters, perform differential gene expression analysis for the selected comparison, and extract statistically significant genes using predefined thresholds for adjusted p-values and log2 fold change. Ask Claude to review the analysis code and verify that the statistical design and filtering criteria have been applied correctly.

nodes.label: Write the Step 4 header and outline the DESeq2 pipeline task
nodes.detail: Back in the R Markdown file, the participant announces the move to differential expression analysis and recaps that the QC showed no bias effects and the expected biology at the clustering and PCA level. They add a '## Step 4: Differential expression analysis (contrast and thresholds)' header, a bold sub-heading 'Run DESeq2 pipeline (size factors, dispersions and model fitting)' with an empty R chunk beneath it, and then select the sub-heading text to copy it for Claude.

nodes.label: Ask Claude for the core DESeq2 pipeline code
nodes.detail: The participant asks Claude's desktop chat for code to run the DESeq2 pipeline (size factors, dispersions, model fitting) that fits into his existing flow.

nodes.label: Insert the DESeq() and dispersion-diagnostic code as a new Step 4 section
nodes.detail: Claude inserts a code block calling DESeq(dds), sizeFactors(dds), plotDispEsts(dds), and resultsNames(dds), explaining that DESeq() wraps the size-factor, dispersion, and Wald-test steps, and shares the updated .Rmd.

nodes.label: Run the DESeq2 model fit and inspect size factors, dispersion, and model coefficients
nodes.detail: The participant runs DESeq(dds) in RStudio, watches the console step through size-factor/dispersion/model-fitting stages, checks sizeFactors(dds), and reviews the plotDispEsts diagnostic plot showing the expected gene-wise-to-fitted-to-final shrinkage trend, then confirms the 'dex_trt_vs_untrt' coefficient via resultsNames(dds).

user_response.label: adopt
user_response.reasoning: In d2 the participant asks Claude for the core DESeq2 pipeline code, so d2 is the source node. AI responds in d3 by inserting a DESeq() block as a new Step 4 section, so d3 is the target AI node. In d4 the participant runs Claude's code exactly as provided with no edits so the label is adopt.

nodes.label: Ask Claude for code to define contrasts and extract results
nodes.detail: The participant asks Claude to give code to 'define contrasts and extract results'.

nodes.label: Insert results()/lfcShrink() code as Step 5 of the script
nodes.detail: Claude inserts code extracting the treatment contrast with results(dds, contrast=c('dex','trt','untrt'), alpha=0.05), ordering by padj, and applying lfcShrink(type='apeglm') for stable effect sizes, explaining why alpha and the apeglm coefficient name matter.

nodes.label: Run the results extraction and inspect the shrunken results table
nodes.detail: The participant runs the returned code, inspects summary(res)/head(res) and the ordered, shrunken resLFC table (baseMean, log2FoldChange, lfcSE, pvalue, padj), and exports the full ordered table to CSV.

user_response.label: adopt
user_response.reasoning: again, the user just adopts the AI code (d6) directly and satisfies with the result, so the label is adopt.

nodes.label: Order and export the full shrunken results table to CSV
nodes.detail: Under a new 'Order and export full results' heading, the participant writes a chunk that orders resLFC by adjusted p-value into res_ordered and saves it with write.csv(as.data.frame(res_ordered), file = "airway_DESeq2_results.csv"), so the complete DE results table is exported.

nodes.label: Ask Claude to convert Ensembl IDs to gene symbols
nodes.detail: The participant asks Claude's desktop chat for code to 'convert ens to symbols'.

nodes.label: Insert mapIds()-based gene-symbol annotation code
nodes.detail: Claude inserts code using org.Hs.eg.db and mapIds() to add SYMBOL and ENTREZID columns to resLFC (keytype='ENSEMBL', multiVals='first'), plus a check counting unmapped genes, and shares the updated file.

nodes.label: Run the annotation code and narrate final results interpretation
nodes.detail: The participant runs the mapIds() code, re-exports the annotated results table, and narrates the meaning of log2 fold-change direction and the importance of using the adjusted p-value over the raw p-value.

user_response.label: adopt
user_response.reasoning: adopt but two more line code not required!!!

Step 5.step_action: Use the quality-controlled expression data and DESeq2 results to create clear visual summaries of the analysis, including a PCA plot, MA plot, volcano plot, and a heatmap of selected differentially expressed genes. Ask Claude to review the plotting code and suggest improvements to the figure labels, statistical annotations, readability, and overall presentation, then apply only scientifically appropriate recommendations. Finally, knit the completed R Markdown document into an HTML report and review the rendered output.

nodes.label: Ask Claude for a publication-level volcano plot with top labelled genes
nodes.detail: The participant asks Claude's desktop chat for a publication-level volcano plot showing the top 10 up- and down-regulated genes in symbol form.

nodes.label: Insert the annotated volcano-plot code
nodes.detail: Claude inserts a ggplot2 block classifying genes as Up/Down/NS by padj<0.05 and |log2FC|>1, labels the top 10 up and top 10 down genes by padj with ggrepel, and applies a colorblind-friendly red/blue/grey palette, explaining the threshold and labeling choices.

nodes.label: Run the volcano plot and interpret the plot
nodes.detail: The participant runs the volcano-plot code in RStudio, reviewing genes such as SPARCL1, DUSP1, and SAMHD1.

nodes.label: Ask for a heatmap of top significant genes
nodes.detail: The participant asks Claude for a heatmap of the top significant genes.

nodes.label: Insert the top-30-gene heatmap code
nodes.detail: Claude inserts pheatmap code pulling VST-normalized expression for the top 30 genes by padj, relabelling rows with gene symbols, annotating columns by dex and cell line, and using a diverging RdBu palette.

nodes.label: Explain the heatmap as a complementary view of the volcano plot
nodes.detail: While Claude generates the heatmap code, the participant switches back to RStudio and explains that the heatmap will show the same information as the volcano plot in a different form, describing the two as complementary ways of seeing the data.

nodes.label: Run the heatmap
nodes.detail: The participant runs the heatmap code, producing the 'Top 30 differentially expressed genes' figure clearly separating treated from untreated samples.

user_response.label: modify
user_response.reasoning: enlarges the figure size to 10 by 10 (modify)

nodes.label: Request an MA plot
nodes.detail: The participant asks Claude for an MA plot.

nodes.label: Insert the MA-plot code reusing the volcano-plot's significance data
nodes.detail: Claude inserts a ggplot2 MA-plot block (log2FoldChange vs. log10-scaled baseMean) that reuses the same volcanoData/topGenes objects and color scheme as the volcano plot for visual consistency.

nodes.label: Run the MA plot and recap the full analysis workflow before knitting
nodes.detail: The participant runs the MA-plot code, producing 'MA plot: dexamethasone-treated vs. untreated' with labelled genes (SPARCL1, DUSP1, SAMHD1, etc.), and remarks that PCA, volcano, heatmap, and MA plot are complementary views of the same results before moving to the final report.

nodes.label: Knit the R Markdown document into an HTML report
nodes.detail: The participant clicks Knit; RStudio's Render pane shows 'processing file: Minnesota_final.Rmd' progressing chunk by chunk (e.g. '71% [unnamed-chunk-15]') until the full report compiles.

nodes.label: Review the rendered report and recap the full workflow
nodes.detail: The participant opens Minnesota_final.html, navigates its table of contents (Preparatory steps, Step 1-5, Session info), confirms the biological-background text and all four result figures rendered correctly, and narrates a recap tying together sample clustering, filtering, dispersion estimates, differential expression, and visualizations, ending with the Session Info section for reproducibility.
